system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Kernelization and branch-and-reduce
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Kernel definitions and branch-and-reduce. Independent-set reductions (degree-1, degree-2 fold, crown, LP) and their correctness arguments.

ATOMS:
- CS-ALG-C06-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: A kernelization for a parameterized problem $L$ is a polynomial-time procedure that maps an instance $(x,k)$ to an instance $(x',k')$ such that $(x',k')\in L \Leftrightarrow (x,k)\in L$ and $|x'|+k' \le f(k)$, where $f$ is a computable function.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0111-s12] More formally, given an binary encoded instance (x,k) ∈{0,1}∗× N of some parameterized problem L, a kernelization for L produces an instance (x′,k′) in polynomial time that satisﬁes: (x′,k′) ∈L ⇔(x,k) ∈L and |x′|+ k′ ≤f(k) where f is a computable function.
- CS-ALG-C06-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Branch-and-reduce algorithms are exact algorithms for parameterized problems that combine data reductions with branching.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0111-s17] Many exact algorithms for parameterized problems combine these data reductions with branching.
    [CS-ALG-p0111-s18] These algorithms are called branch-and-reduce algorithms.
- CS-ALG-C06-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: Data reduction rules reduce the size of a graph while retaining the ability to compute an optimal solution.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0111-s09] Data reduction rules, or simply reductions, reduce the size of a graph while retaining the ability to compute an optimal solution.
- CS-ALG-C06-S2-01.r1a | S2
  ATOM: The degree-1 reduction rule for maximum independent set (MIS) removes each vertex $v$ of degree one together with its neighbor, because $v$ is always in at least one MIS.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0112-s21] We illustrate this by brieﬂy covering the degree-1 and degree-2 vertex fold reduction rules: (1) In the degree-1 reduction rule (see Fig. 1) one removes vertices v of degree one (and their neighbors), as they are always in at least one MIS.
- CS-ALG-C06-S2-01.r1b | S2
  ATOM: For a degree-1 vertex $v$ with neighbor $w$, a maximum independent set $I$ must contain $v$ or $w$, since otherwise $I\cup\{v\}$ would be an independent set of larger cardinality.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0112-s21] We illustrate this by brieﬂy covering the degree-1 and degree-2 vertex fold reduction rules: (1) In the degree-1 reduction rule (see Fig. 1) one removes vertices v of degree one (and their neighbors), as they are always in at least one MIS.
    [CS-ALG-p0112-s22] To see this, note that v or its neighbor w must be in some MIS I, otherwise I ∪{v} is an independent set of larger cardinality.
- CS-ALG-C06-S2-01.r1c | S2
  ATOM: For a degree-1 vertex $v$ with neighbor $w$, if a maximum independent set $I$ contains $w$, then removing $w$ from $I$ and adding $v$ yields an independent set of the same size.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0112-s21] We illustrate this by brieﬂy covering the degree-1 and degree-2 vertex fold reduction rules: (1) In the degree-1 reduction rule (see Fig. 1) one removes vertices v of degree one (and their neighbors), as they are always in at least one MIS.
    [CS-ALG-p0112-s23] If w is in I, one can obtain an independent set of the same size by removing w from I and adding v instead. (2) For the degree-2 vertex fold (see Fig. 2) one removes vertices v with exactly two neighbors u and w that are not adjacent to each other.
- CS-ALG-C06-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: A branch-and-reduce algorithm first applies reduction rules exhaustively, until no further reductions are possible or they are prohibitively expensive. It then picks an edge or vertex and branches into one subproblem per possible state of that element. It continues reducing and branching in each subproblem and returns the best result over all branches.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0111-s19] First, the algorithm aims to reduce the graph size by exhaustively applying reduction rules until there are no further data reductions possible or they are prohibitively expensive.
    [CS-ALG-p0111-s20] Then, the algorithm picks an edge e ∈E (or a vertex v ∈V, depending on the problem) and branches the problem into multiple subproblems, one subproblem for each potential state of e in regard to the problem.
    [CS-ALG-p0111-s22] The branch-and-reduce algorithm then continues to apply reduction rules to both of these subproblems and continues branching when there are no further reductions possible.
    [CS-ALG-p0111-s23] The branch-and-reduce algorithm returns the best result over all branches.

  ATOM: In the degree-2 vertex fold for the maximum independent set problem, a vertex $v$ with exactly two neighbors $u$ and $w$ that are not adjacent to each other is removed and a new vertex $v'$ is inserted and connected to the union of the neighborhoods of $u$ and $w$, which reduces the graph size by two vertices.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0112-s23] If w is in I, one can obtain an independent set of the same size by removing w from I and adding v instead. (2) For the degree-2 vertex fold (see Fig. 2) one removes vertices v with exactly two neighbors u and w that are not adjacent to each other.
